extracted.intended_audience: agency officials, administrative law practitioners, policymakers, and legal counsel concerned with notice-and-comment rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal analysis on identifying, evaluating, and responding to malattributed (false-identity) and mass/computer-generated public comments in federal notice-and-comment rulemakings, including criminal statute applicability, APA obligations, harms, and mitigation steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fraud prosecution elements for malattributed comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Malattributed comments can meet some elements of fraud (they involve a false statement of fact), but several elements—especially agency "reliance" on the identity, and proof of actual injury—are difficult to satisfy in run-of-the-mill comment submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because agencies typically do not rely on commenter identity, it will be rare that an agency "relied on" the false identity. Where the false identity is recognizable (e.g., Barack Obama) the agency will recognize the falsehood and not rely on it. If the submitter claims relevant personal experience, the relevant falsehood is the content (the claimed experience) rather than merely the name. Fraud also requires actual injury to the defrauded party; loss of public confidence is arguable but not the tangible harm fraud statutes generally require. Courts require materiality as part of fraud; if identity does not matter to the agency, a malattribution will often be immaterial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wire/mail fraud statutes require obtaining money or property
rubrics_metrics.description: Wire fraud (18 U.S.C. §1343) and mail fraud (18 U.S.C. §1341) typically require that the perpetrator be attempting to obtain 'money or property' from the defrauded party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submission of a comment uses mail or wire, but influencing agency policymaking generally is not an attempt to obtain money or property from the agency, so these statutes are unlikely to apply. See Cleveland v. United States (distinguishing attempts to obtain property).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conspiracy to defraud the United States (18 U.S.C. §371) may reach malattributed comments in some cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 371 criminalizes conspiring to 'defraud the United States, or any agency thereof in any manner or for any purpose,' a broad reading that has covered conspiracies to impair, obstruct, or defeat lawful functions of government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using false identities could amount to a 'trick or deceit' to impair agency functions—for example, making the agency believe many nonexistent individuals support a position, or submitting many comments to slow the agency (an 'obstruct' theory). However, §371 prosecutions historically arise in contexts like tax or disclosure obligations ('Klein conspiracies'); difficulty proving substantial harm to the government and the need to prove conspiracy elements make prosecutions unlikely in typical malattribution cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: False statements statute (18 U.S.C. §1001) applicability and materiality requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: 18 U.S.C. §1001 prohibits making 'false, fictitious, or fraudulent' statements to a federal agency; unlike fraud, it does not require financial loss or reliance, but it does require materiality (the falsehood must be capable of influencing the decisionmaking body).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most elements of §1001 can be satisfied by malattributed comments: they make a false statement, the falsehood can be knowing/willful (the programmer or organizer knows misidentifications occur), and rulemaking is 'a matter within the jurisdiction' of the agency. The key issue is materiality: use of a false name is material only where the identity affects the weight of the comment (e.g., the comment purports to be from someone with unique, relevant expertise or situated experience). Example: SEC proxy-submission controversies where letters were presented as from Main Street investors but were organized/written by an industry group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Materiality of identity is fact-specific; claims of expertise can make a malattribution material
rubrics_metrics.description: A malattributed comment is material under §1001 when it falsely claims to be from someone whose identity or asserted expertise would give the comment more weight (e.g., a Ph.D. researcher, a twenty-year industry employee, a direct user of the regulated product).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a false name conveys background information that could affect the agency's consideration, the falsehood may be material even if the name alone seems innocuous. Such bespoke misrepresentations are harder to detect and more likely to be actionable than generic mass submissions with random names.

rubrics_metrics.name: APA obligation to accept and consider comments (including potentially malattributed ones)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Administrative Procedure Act requires agencies to consider the 'relevant matter presented' and courts demand that agencies respond to all significant comments in final rules; this obligation arguably extends to malattributed comments if they are significant and substantive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under one reading, agencies must accept, review, and respond to malattributed comments like any other. Agencies frequently conclude many comments are insubstantial and need not be answered; a detected malattribution can be a factor supporting non-response. However, whether the APA imposes a duty to accept or reject malattributed comments is unsettled and may turn on whether an agency has published a clear policy about accepting anonymous/malattributed submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agencies may set reasonable requirements for comment form and content (e.g., no anonymous comments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies are free to impose reasonable requirements on the form and content of public comments—deadlines, civility rules, and identity requirements are examples—and to police those requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many agencies already allow or prohibit anonymous comments; prior ACUS recommendations urge agencies to set clear public policies. If an agency has a policy prohibiting anonymous or malattributed comments, it may lawfully refuse them. Examples and citations: accepted practice of ignoring late-filed comments; 2011 ACUS Recommendation that agencies publish policies regarding anonymous comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation (or lack thereof) to 'cleanse' the docket of malattributed comments
rubrics_metrics.description: There is debate whether the APA requires agencies to remove malattributed comments from the docket; purging comments would impose effort and may make judicial review of the full record harder, so removal is not obviously required unless malattributed comments cause affirmative harm beyond mere uselessness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generally, agencies simply ignore comments that make no contribution; removing them is unnecessary and could hinder transparency and review. To justify a mandatory purge, malattributed comments must be 'worse than useless'—e.g., they drown out legitimate comments or mislead about public sentiment in ways that cause affirmative harm. Bespoke, sophisticated 'deep fake' comments are the scenario where removal/cleansing arguments are strongest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether an agency may rely on malattributed comments in decisionmaking (reasoned decisionmaking constraint)
rubrics_metrics.description: The APA's prohibition on arbitrary and capricious action requires reasoned decisionmaking; relying on malattributed comments as a measure of public sentiment or treating false-authority comments as authoritative would be unreasonable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no per se rule either allowing or prohibiting reliance on malattributed comments. If a comment is relevant, factually accurate, and useful, an agency may use it regardless of the name attached. But it would be arbitrary and capricious to treat malattributed comments as reliable indicators of public sentiment or to rely on a comment that purports to be from an authority when it is not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two distinct misleading risks from malattributed comments: identity deception and distorted public sentiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Malattributed comments can mislead by (a) falsely conveying the identity/background of a commenter (identity deception) and (b) making it appear that more commenters hold a position than actually do (distorted public sentiment), especially when computer-generated mass comments are attached to many names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identity deception is typically trivial—agencies rarely notice commenter names—but 'deep fake' bespoke comments claiming expert identities may be misleading. Distorted public sentiment is a central concern with mass/computer-generated malattributed comments: thousands of identical comments with different names can create the false impression of broad public support. Whether agencies treat comments as evidence of public sentiment affects how misleading these are.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harms to individuals whose names are used in malattributed comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Using someone’s name and email address without permission can cause psychological harms (annoyance, anger, distress) and potential reputational harms if a malattributed comment is noticed and judged negatively by third parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Though many victims may never notice or be harmed, a single viral exposure could produce serious reputational injury. Even if the conduct does not meet federal identity-theft statutes, people may reasonably feel victimized. Quantifying these harms is difficult and perceptions will vary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discouraging malattributed comments: notice and criminal-warning approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: E-rulemaking platforms (Regulations.gov) and agencies can discourage malattributed comments by publishing Terms of Participation that (a) encourage commenters to submit their own comments or obtain permission and (b) warn that knowingly making materially false statements about identity may violate federal law (e.g., 18 U.S.C. §1001; subject to 18 U.S.C. §1028(c), unlawful use of another's means of identification).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulations.gov’s user notice explicitly states it is a violation of federal law to knowingly and willfully make materially false statements or to use another person’s means of identification without authority, tying platform terms to criminal statutes. Such notices are a practical, low-cost deterrent and support agency policies requiring clear rules about submission permissibility.
